verdict: PASS WITH NON-BLOCKING OBSERVATIONS -- 0 blockers, 6 non-blocking. This is the stronger of the two instruments reviewed today. Every central claim reproduced under independent measurement; the one self-disclosed weakness is real, is correctly reasoned, and is if anything UNDERSTATED in the author's favour; the drift gate is genuinely two-directional; and the exit discipline is the cleanest defence against litmus defect D-6 in the corpus. The findings below are gaps in DISCLOSURE and in one ungated divergence axis, not defects in the repair.

theProcessGuardDesign.question: Executing v4's pinned bytes in-process with a fake `subprocess` installed in sys.modules -- sound, or a new forgery surface?
theProcessGuardDesign.verdict: SOUND, with one structural consequence the author names and one the author does not.
whyItIsSound: Executing rather than transcribing is section 7.8's own rule ('an instrument that transcribes is testing its transcription') and section 7.3's ('executing a verified closure is not building against it'). Reimplementing v4's 2136 lines would have been the worse design by the corpus's own doctrine.

The guard's capability surface is minimal and was probed directly. `run` is the only method; every other attribute name raises ExternalProcessRefused by __getattr__ with the operation NAMED, never an opaque AttributeError. Verified: guard.Popen -> 'refused attribute: subprocess.Popen'; guard.check_output -> 'refused attribute: subprocess.check_output'; guard.run with a foreign argv -> 'refused: run argv=(...)'.

The one permitted invocation is DERIVED FROM v2's AST rather than transcribed -- derive_enumeration_invocation returns ('rg','--files','docs/coop/artifacts') with kwargs {capture_output, check, cwd, text}, and refuses if v2 contains anything other than exactly one external invocation of the expected shape. Verified: appending a second subprocess.run(['curl',...]) to v2 produces exit 1 RPPV5-CLOSURE-UNEXPECTED-INVOCATION; changing v2's enumeration root to /etc produces exit 1. This is section 7.8 move 2 applied correctly.
The argv, the kwarg SET, and the kwarg VALUES are all checked -- check/capture_output/text must each be exactly True. A weakened-flags invocation is refused (probe 22).
sys.modules is restored in a finally block whether or not `subprocess` was previously imported. Verified by direct test.

The guard's replacement data is not invented: it is two independently written standard-library walks, cross-checked against each other and against a repeat of the first, with up to 3 retries so that a file arriving mid-walk in a live tree is not misread as an enumerator disagreement. Only a disagreement that SURVIVES retries becomes RPPV5-ENUM-DISAGREE.

The subject asserts its OWN zero-external-process property mechanically against its own bytes (RPPV5-SELF-EXTERNAL-PROCESS, 0 rows) and proves the scanner is non-vacuous with 8 dirty probes that must all fire and 3 clean probes that must not. Measured 8/8 every run.
theProcessGuardDesign.theStructuralConsequenceTheAuthorNAMES: The guard is a data-injection point by construction: v5 decides what v4 sees. The author's answer is that the injected data is cross-checked between two independent walkers and its digest is published in the banner (enumeration_sha256, enumeration_variants). That is the right mitigation and it is disclosed.
theProcessGuardDesign.theStructuralConsequenceTheAuthorDOESNOT: The two walkers are cross-checked against EACH OTHER, never against `rg --files`. They therefore catch an implementation bug in one walker and CANNOT catch a shared semantic divergence from the tool they stand in for -- because both encode the same authoring decisions. One such divergence exists and is ungated: see finding RPPV5-N1 (hidden files).
theProcessGuardDesign.isItANewForgerySurface: NO, in the sense that matters. The closure whose behaviour the guard shapes is hash-pinned at V4_SHA256, so nobody can write code that exploits the guard without tripping RPPV5-PIN-DRIFT. Verified: appending one comment to v4 produces exit 1, RPPV5-PIN-DRIFT, no traceback. The guard cannot be reached by an attacker; it can only be wrong on the author's behalf, which is what the enumeration cross-checks and the published digest exist to bound.

theNPA4FalsePositive.facts: check-narrative-packet-agreement.py NPA-4 derives externalTools by static AST closure over exec/importlib edges. Measured on the live tree: externalToolDependents 4, externalTools ['curl','rg']. v5 is one of the 4. Both attributions are false: v5 starts no process, and `rg` reaches it only because it executes v2's bytes under a runtime stand-in that a static scan cannot see. `curl` reaches it from a byte-string literal inside v5's own mutation suite at line 837 -- b"import subprocess\nsubprocess.run(['curl','https://x'])\n" -- which is a NEGATIVE probe proving derive_enumeration_invocation refuses a foreign invocation shape.
theNPA4FalsePositive.isItDocumented: YES, in IMPLEMENTER-BLUEPRINT.md around line 721, in a dedicated table row and a caution paragraph. NPA currently exits 0 because the blueprint records the truth, so the agreement check passes: the false positive is RECORDED, not resolved.
theNPA4FalsePositive.gradeOfTheJudgement: MOSTLY RIGHT, AND ONE STEP TOO FAR.
theNPA4FalsePositive.whatIsRight: The principle the blueprint states -- 'When a checker and reality disagree, find out which is wrong before repairing either' -- is exactly correct, and the alternative would have been to make a document assert a dependency v5 does not have. Greener and wrong. Refusing to tune the artifact to satisfy an instrument is the same discipline that produced the whole successor-instrument doctrine, and the author also declined to weaken NPA-4, which is the other tempting shortcut. Both refusals are right.
theNPA4FalsePositive.whatIsOneStepTooFar: The principle applies to facts about reality. WHICH TOOL NAME appears in a negative probe is not a fact about reality -- it is an arbitrary authoring choice, and a different choice preserves the test exactly. I verified this: derive_enumeration_invocation refuses b"subprocess.run(['curl','https://x'])", b"subprocess.run(['xyzzy','https://x'])" and b"subprocess.run(['TOOL','ARG'])" IDENTICALLY -- all three trip the `len(argv) != 3` shape check. Choosing 'curl' bought the test nothing and cost a permanent false entry in a derived, machine-maintained dependency census that other lanes and future SBOM/static-analysis passes will read, inside a file whose own banner asserts external_processes=0. The cost is small and the mitigation (documenting it) is real; but the author's stated reason -- refusing to make a document lie -- does not cover this case, because no document would have lied.
theNPA4FalsePositive.netGrade: Sound instinct, correct outcome for the `rg` half (which is genuinely irreducible: a runtime stand-in is invisible to a static scan, section 7.6's shape), over-applied to the `curl` half (which was avoidable at zero cost to the probe's power). Non-blocking.

A bare `except Exception` at the top of the try block converts any internal failure into RPPV5-INTERNAL with the file:line of the last frame, exit 3, and the explicit sentence 'this instrument failed to complete; that is NOT a verdict about the artifacts'. section710Compliance.verdict: COMPLIANT ON THE NAMING REQUIREMENT, RESIDUAL ON THE EXIT-CODE REQUIREMENT.
section710Compliance.detail: Section 7.10's prescription for a kept digest pin is 'a named, NON-FATAL drift notice distinguishable from a semantic failure, so a reader can tell the two apart without reading the source'. v5's pin drift is NAMED (RPPV5-PIN-DRIFT on stderr line 1, with a two-line explanation) and distinguishable WITHOUT reading the source -- but it is exit 1, the same status as a semantic finding. A process gating on exit status alone cannot separate 'the pinned predecessor advanced' from 'the artifacts are wrong'.
section710Compliance.isThatDefensible: YES, on the author's own reasoning, which is stated at the PinDrift class: a pinned checker's bytes are a statement about bytes, section 7.2 binds verdicts to bytes, so drift is a finding rather than an environment problem. Section 7.10 itself says 'a pinned digest is the right instrument for bytes that must never change', and a reviewed checker under sections 7.2/7.6 is exactly that class. v5 partitions coherently: ENVIRONMENT -> 3, BYTES -> 1.
section710Compliance.theResidualThatRemains: v5 inherits v4's pins over ARTIFACTS, and artifacts are the class section 7.10 says the corpus is explicitly waiting to change. When rust-provider-protocol.v4.json legitimately advances, v5 goes to exit 1 with five hash-mismatch rows -- the check-versioning-v14 failure mode section 7.10 records. v5 cannot fix this without reimplementing v4, which section 7.8 forbids; the cost is correctly pushed to a successor. What v5 DOES add, and it is the right mitigation, is RPPV5-ENUMERATION-NOT-REACHED, which tells the reader in one line that the enumeration invariants did not run and names the cause -- section 7.10's 'when an instrument fails early, ask what it was also protecting', answered by the instrument itself instead of by a reader.

nonBlocking.title: A SECOND latent divergence axis from `rg --files` exists, is ungated, and is undisclosed: ripgrep's hidden-file default
nonBlocking.severity: non-blocking, LATENT today (0 dotfiles and 0 symlinks currently under docs/coop/artifacts)
nonBlocking.detail: The docstring discloses and the instrument gates exactly one divergence axis -- ignore rules -- and concludes 'This checker's enumeration is ignore-independent BY CONSTRUCTION ... so what this repair removes is a latent environment dependency.' True, and incomplete. `rg --files` also omits DOTFILES by default (--hidden defaults to false). A stdlib walk includes them. Being ignore-independent does not make an enumeration `rg --files`-equivalent.
nonBlocking.measured: In a scratch tree containing normal.json, .hidden-artifact.json, sub/nested.json, a symlinked file and a symlinked directory: `rg --files` returned 2 paths (normal.json, sub/nested.json); v5's walk_pathlib and walk_scandir each returned 3, including .hidden-artifact.json. Then on the frozen 527-file tree: dropping a single .zz-hidden.json moved v5's enumeration from 527 / sha 30a476d270835b08 to 528 / sha 32b0326ea6dcf55d while `rg --files` still reported 527 -- and v5 exited 0 with no finding. The gated axis behaves correctly by contrast: a .gitignore carrying one pattern produced exit 1 with active_ignore_patterns=1.
nonBlocking.notAlsoAProblemForSymlinks: Symlinks ARE covered, differently and loudly: walk_scandir records them as irregular and RPPV5-ENUM-NONREGULAR fires at exit 1. Verified.
nonBlocking.whyItMatters: The two walkers cross-check each other, so a shared semantic decision -- include dotfiles -- is invisible to the cross-check by construction. This is the concrete instance of the structural consequence noted under theProcessGuardDesign. Practical blast radius today is near zero because v4's verdict is insensitive to the enumeration anyway (measured above), so the exposure is to the DISCLOSURE, not to the verdict.
nonBlocking.repairShape: A successor could count non-ignored dotfiles under the subtree and gate it at 0 exactly as activeInRepoIgnorePatterns is gated, or state in the banner that the enumeration is a SUPERSET of `rg --files` by two named rules rather than an equivalent.

whatAGreenRUNofThisInstrumentMeans: That the pinned bytes are the reviewed bytes and drift stops the run; that v4's entire check set executed to a verdict in an environment where v4 alone cannot start; that every recorded execution figure in the response artifact equals what this run actually measured and equals what the candidate documents themselves derive, three ways; that all six register-bound artifacts hash as recorded; and that this instrument started zero external processes, asserted against its own AST. It does NOT mean the artifacts' prose is true -- 108 of 252 narrative leaves admit an appended falsehood undetected once pins are re-pointed, and the instrument prints that number with its definition in its own banner. Freeze section 7.8's bound applies in full and the instrument states it verbatim.
recommendation: ACCEPT. The repair is real, narrowly scoped, and does what it says: it converts three checkers that could not run in this environment into a verdict, without editing any reviewed byte and without reimplementing anything. The dispatch asked whether an instrument that fakes a stdlib module for code it executes deserves hard scrutiny -- it does, it received it here, and it held: the closure it feeds is hash-pinned, the capability surface is one method and refuses everything else by name, the injected data is derived from two independent walkers and its digest is published, and the one thing the guard cannot self-check is named in finding RPPV5-N1. Whether claim-register.v1.json should be re-pointed from check-rust-provider-protocol-v4.py to this file is a coordinator decision this review does not make; it notes only that the register currently names a validator which, measured, cannot run here.
